whyItExists.problem: Every application needs to create and retrieve data. MongoDB's insert and find operations are the foundation of all database work. Understanding filters, projections, cursors, and query operators is essential for building any real application.
whyItExists.solution: MongoDB provides insertOne, insertMany for writes, and find/findOne for reads. The find() method accepts a filter object and a projection object, giving you fine-grained control over which documents and which fields to return.
whyItExists.whenToUse: insertOne for single-document writes, insertMany for batch imports. find() for listing and searching, findOne() for looking up a single document by ID or unique field.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use find() without a filter on large collections — it returns all documents and can overwhelm your application. Always add a filter or at least a .limit().

explainModes.beginner: insert is like adding a new row to a spreadsheet. find is like searching the spreadsheet. With MongoDB, you just pass a JSON object describing what you're looking for, like { name: 'Alice' } to find everyone named Alice.
explainModes.simple: insertOne() adds a single document. insertMany() adds multiple at once. find() searches for documents matching a filter. findOne() returns just the first match. Add a projection to control which fields come back.
explainModes.standard: MongoDB's read operations use filter objects for query predicates and projection objects for field selection. find() returns a cursor — a lazy iterator — which you call .toArray() or iterate with for-await-of. Query operators like $gt, $in, and $regex allow complex filtering.
explainModes.technical: find() sends a query to the MongoDB server which applies the filter, projection, sort, skip, and limit server-side before returning results. The cursor object in the driver is lazy — it only fetches documents when iterated. MongoDB uses index scan (IXSCAN) when suitable indexes exist, otherwise falls back to COLLSCAN.
explainModes.deepDive: MongoDB's query planner evaluates multiple query plans in parallel using a 'trial period' — it runs all candidate plans and picks the fastest (by number of keys examined or documents examined). The winning plan is cached in the plan cache keyed by the query shape. Projections are pushed down to the storage engine — with covered queries (all projected fields in an index), MongoDB never reads documents at all, only the index.

content.text: MongoDB provides two insert methods: insertOne() for a single document and insertMany() for multiple documents at once. Both return an acknowledgement with the inserted _id(s).
insertMany() is much faster than calling insertOne() in a loop — it sends all documents in a single network request. For bulk imports, use insertMany() with batches of 500–1000 documents.

find() returns a cursor — a lazy iterator over matching documents. Call .toArray() to get all results as an array, or iterate with for await...of for memory-efficient streaming. Use findOne() to get just the first matching document.
MongoDB provides comparison and logical operators to build complex queries. Prefix operators with $.
A projection is the second argument to find(). Use 1 to include a field and 0 to exclude it. You cannot mix inclusions and exclusions (except for _id).

Avoid large skip() values for pagination — MongoDB must scan and discard all skipped documents. For large datasets, use cursor-based pagination instead: query documents where _id > lastSeenId (much more efficient).

questions.question: What does a projection do in MongoDB?
options: Selects which fields to include or exclude in results
questions.explanation: Projections control which fields appear in the query result — use 1 to include and 0 to exclude. The filter (first argument) controls which documents are returned.

questions.question: Which operator finds documents where price is between 500 and 1000?
questions.explanation: MongoDB uses $gte (greater than or equal) and $lte (less than or equal) operators. There is no $between operator.

questions.question: What does find() return?
options: A Promise that resolves to null
questions.explanation: find() returns a Cursor — a lazy iterator. Call .toArray() to fetch all results, or iterate with for-await-of for memory-efficient streaming of large result sets.

faq.q: How do I find documents by _id?
faq.a: Use findOne({ _id: new ObjectId('507f1f77bcf86cd799439011') }) — you must wrap the hex string in ObjectId(). Without the wrapper, MongoDB will compare the string to the ObjectId, which never matches.

faq.q: What is the difference between find() and findOne()?
faq.a: find() returns a cursor over all matching documents. findOne() returns just the first matching document (or null if none found). Use findOne() when you expect exactly one result, like a user by email.

faq.q: How do I count documents without returning them?
faq.a: Use collection.countDocuments(filter) for an accurate count with a filter, or collection.estimatedDocumentCount() for a fast approximate total count of the whole collection.

usedIn: User profile lookups in social apps
examples: Building a product search API: find({ $text: { $search: query }, inStock: true }).sort({ score: -1 }).limit(20)
User authentication: findOne({ email: input.email }) — then verify password hash
